clue.text: Be fat for a change, before you start to waste away

indicators.note: the shuffled letters come before the next piece in the answer
doing something for a change means doing it differently, so these letters are rearranged
the start of the word is its opening letter only

explanation.surface: A dieter is told to get fat for once before wasting away.
explanation.walkthrough: 'for a change' turns BEFAT into TABEF; 'before' puts it ahead of Y, the start of 'you'.
explanation.definitionFit: Tabefy is a rare verb meaning to emaciate or waste away, from the Latin for wasting disease.

clue.text: Conceited character given to display

parts.note: an advertisement is a display, shortened to ad

explanation.surface: A vain person is prone to showing off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'given' is a link word. Toad of Toad Hall, from Kenneth Grahame's The Wind in the Willows, is famously boastful.
explanation.definitionFit: Mr Toad in The Wind in the Willows is the classic vain, boastful character of children's literature.

clue.text: Merseyside force to deal with moonshine

parts.note: Bootle is a town in Merseyside, near Liverpool
g is the symbol for the force of gravity, as in g-force

explanation.surface: A police force in Merseyside cracks down on illegal liquor.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Merseyside force' reads as a police force, but splits into a Merseyside town and a physics symbol. BOOTLE is a town just north of Liverpool.
explanation.definitionFit: To bootleg is to make or trade illicit liquor, the moonshine of Prohibition days.

clue.text: When foreign soldier turned out with nothing on

indicators.note: out means those letters are taken out of the word foreign
turned means the soldier's two letters are read the other way round

parts.note: GI is an American soldier
nothing is zero, the letter O

explanation.surface: A question about when a foreign soldier appeared in the nude.
explanation.walkthrough: 'turned' flips the soldier's letters before 'out' removes them from the printed word. 'When' is the definition, a time of day.
explanation.definitionFit: The forenoon is the morning, a time that answers the question when.

clue.text: Cut off a partner who's out of place

indicators.note: the partner stands outside the word for place, which is held within it

parts.note: a mate is a partner
to put is to place

explanation.surface: Someone cuts off a partner who doesn't fit in.
explanation.walkthrough: 'out of place' looks like one phrase meaning misplaced; 'out of' is the container signal and 'place' is PUT.
explanation.definitionFit: To amputate is to cut off a limb surgically.

clue.text: Making free with endless music playing in a large building

indicators.note: the scrambled letters go inside the building

parts.note: a mansion is a large house

indicators.note: playing suggests the letters are performed in a new way, so they are rearranged
endless means the last letter of the word music is dropped

explanation.surface: A party in a stately home makes free with music playing nonstop.
explanation.walkthrough: 'endless' drops the last letter of the printed word, 'playing' rearranges what is left, and 'in' sets that inside the building. 'Making free' is a noun phrase, the act of freeing.
explanation.definitionFit: Manumission is the formal act of freeing a slave, so making someone free.

clue.text: What setters get from trying to make clues right?

definitions.text: What setters get from trying to make clues right?

indicators.note: trying to make something of letters means working them into a new order

explanation.surface: A setter's reward for the stress of perfecting clues.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is the definition and the wordplay: 'trying to make' rearranges CLUES with R.
explanation.definitionFit: Stomach ulcers are popularly blamed on the stress of demanding work such as setting crosswords.

clue.text: Dodgy dealing made straight

indicators.note: dodgy means crooked, so the letters are not in their proper order

explanation.surface: Crooked trading has been set straight.
explanation.definitionFit: Aligned means put in a straight line, so made straight.

clue.text: Teatime in 3?

parts.note: 3 is the forenoon, so a break for tea in the morning is the snack meant

explanation.surface: A question about when to take tea in the morning.
explanation.walkthrough: 3 refers to the answer at 3 down, the morning. Elevenses is a British mid-morning snack of tea and biscuits.
explanation.definitionFit: Elevenses is a light refreshment taken around eleven in the morning, the forenoon's teatime.

clue.text: Affairs of 3 appertaining to the Guardian

parts.note: 3 down is the forenoon, the morning, abbreviated AM
the clue appeared in the Guardian, so what belongs to the paper is ours

explanation.surface: Gossip about the morning love affairs reported in the Guardian.
explanation.walkthrough: 3 points to the answer at 3 down, the morning, so AM.
explanation.definitionFit: Amours are love affairs, the word borrowed from French.

clue.text: Fashionable writer may do it at book launch

definitions.text: may do it at book launch

parts.note: in means fashionable, as in the in thing
a scribe is a writer

explanation.surface: A trendy author signs copies at a book launch.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fashionable writer' reads as one person, the author, but splits into two pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Authors inscribe copies of their book for buyers at a launch event.

clue.text: Apple in battle with IT brand

parts.note: Blenheim was a 1704 battle won by Marlborough
Orange was a British mobile phone and internet brand

explanation.surface: Apple competes with another technology brand.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Apple' looks like the tech company in a brand battle, but it is a fruit: Blenheim Orange is an English apple variety.
explanation.definitionFit: Blenheim Orange is a traditional English variety of eating and cooking apple.

clue.text: Unknown depicted orally as global business

indicators.note: orally means the words are spoken, giving the sound of the answer

parts.note: an unknown is X in algebra, spelt ex, and depicted is portrayed

explanation.surface: A mystery figure is described in speech as an international business.
explanation.walkthrough: 'orally' says EX PORTRAYED aloud.
explanation.definitionFit: The export trade is business selling goods abroad, so commerce on a global scale.

clue.text: Ransome's air mail?

parts.note: Arthur Ransome wrote a novel about birds carrying messages, and that is post by air

explanation.surface: A question about letters sent by air in an Arthur Ransome book.
explanation.walkthrough: Arthur Ransome's children's novel of 1936 bears this title; homing birds carry messages, mail by air.
explanation.definitionFit: Carrier birds deliver messages through the air, the earliest airborne post.

clue.text: Bits of some crumbled slice

parts.note: part means some, a portion

indicators.note: crumbled means broken up, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Fragments of a broken slice of bread.
explanation.walkthrough: 'crumbled' turns SLICE into ICLES.
explanation.definitionFit: Particles are tiny pieces or bits of matter.

clue.text: Troubles with splashback

indicators.note: back means the word is read backwards

parts.note: a splash of soda is the mixer added to whisky

explanation.surface: Trouble caused by liquid splashing back.
explanation.walkthrough: 'splashback' reads as one word, the panel behind a sink; it splits into 'splash' (SODA) and 'back'.
explanation.definitionFit: Ados are fusses or troubles, as in much ado about nothing.

clue.text: Yesteryear's pop swamps listener with coarse language

indicators.note: the music engulfs the listener, holding it inside

parts.note: swing was the popular music of the 1930s and 1940s
an ear is the organ that listens

explanation.surface: Old pop music drowns out a listener with crude lyrics.
explanation.definitionFit: Swearing is the use of profanity, coarse language.

clue.text: Packed soundly and transported

indicators.note: soundly means as said aloud, giving a word that sounds the same

parts.note: packed in paper is wrapped

explanation.surface: Parcels well packed and sent on their way.
explanation.walkthrough: 'soundly' looks like it means thoroughly; it signals the sound of WRAPPED.
explanation.definitionFit: Rapt means carried away with delight, transported in the emotional sense.

clue.text: Errant knight has a row with mate

parts.note: a pal is a mate
din means a loud row, a racket

explanation.surface: A wandering knight quarrels with his friend.
explanation.walkthrough: 'with' puts the mate first.
explanation.definitionFit: A paladin was one of Charlemagne's champions, the archetype of the wandering knight.

clue.text: Spooner's actor with native Americans leads to great ideas

indicators.note: Spooner's means the first sounds of the two words are swapped

parts.note: John Wayne was an actor in westerns
braves are Native American warriors

explanation.surface: A western star alongside Native American warriors inspires great ideas.
explanation.walkthrough: Swapping the first sounds of WAYNE and BRAVES gives BRAYNE WAVES; the phrase is spelt as brain and waves.
explanation.definitionFit: A brainwave is a sudden clever idea or inspiration.

clue.text: Good plonk given at random

indicators.note: at random means in no order, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Cheap wine handed out haphazardly.
explanation.walkthrough: Plonk is British slang for cheap wine; a fine wine of a good year is the opposite, used tongue in cheek.
explanation.definitionFit: Vintage wine is from a single good year, so a fine wine.

clue.text: Tom going to the doctor?

parts.note: a tomcat hunts mice, and a doctor's surgery is a place one goes; the cat is out hunting mice

explanation.surface: A man called Tom on his way to see his GP.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tom' looks like a man's name; it is a male cat. The cat that goes after mice is a ratter of rodents.
explanation.definitionFit: A mouser is a cat skilled at catching mice, like the tom.

clue.text: The wages of sin?

parts.note: Romans says the wages of sin is death; here the phrase is read as money earned by wrongdoing

explanation.surface: A biblical reflection on the reward for sin.
explanation.walkthrough: The Bible says the wages of sin is death; the question reads it as literal pay for wrongdoing.
explanation.definitionFit: Profits obtained dishonestly are what a sinner earns, literally the pay of wrongdoing.

clue.text: Lady's disease, lacking exercise

indicators.note: lacking means without, so the exercise letters are taken away

parts.note: herpes is a viral disease
PE is physical education, exercise at school

explanation.surface: A woman's ailment caused by too little exercise.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lady's' looks like a possessive adjective on the disease, but it is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Hers is the possessive pronoun for a woman, meaning belonging to a lady.

clue.text: Eliot's boy is brought to justice

parts.note: a lad is a boy
law means justice

explanation.surface: A poet's son is taken to court.
explanation.walkthrough: 'brought to' is a link. Will Ladislaw is a character in George Eliot's Middlemarch.
explanation.definitionFit: Will Ladislaw is the young hero of George Eliot's novel Middlemarch.

clue.text: Stretch to analyse detail

indicators.note: to analyse is to break something down, so the letters are broken up and rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone takes time to analyse the detail.
explanation.definitionFit: To dilate is to widen or stretch, as pupils do.

clue.text: Why washing lines are used for various items?

definitions.meaning: washing is hung out because the ... it, read as a two-word sentence
odds and ends of miscellaneous goods

explanation.definitionFit: Sundries are miscellaneous small items too various to list.

clue.text: Mounds in the commentary box?

definitions.meaning: an agger is a Roman earthwork or rampart, a mound
Jonathan Agnew, a BBC cricket radio commentator, is known by this nickname

explanation.definitionFit: Aggers are Roman embankments; it is also Jonathan Agnew's nickname on BBC cricket radio.
